title: Welcome to the Agency
description: Your first hour at **Brightline Media**: how we are organised, who does what, how a project moves through the building, and where to find things when you are stuck.
objectives: Describe what Brightline Media does and who its clients are
Name the four departments and what each one owns
Explain how a campaign moves from brief to report
Know where to look for information before asking

modules.title: Welcome to the agency
modules.instructions: Six short cards to get you oriented at Brightline Media.

cards.title: Hello, and welcome to Brightline Media
cards.body:
We're a performance marketing agency of **48 people** across Lisbon and Tallinn.

Over the next few minutes you'll meet the teams, learn how a campaign moves through the agency, and pick up the one rule every account runs on.

cards.title: Three teams, one scoreboard
cards.body:
**Strategy** shapes the plan and owns the client relationship.

**Creative** turns the plan into ads, landing pages and copy that earn attention.

**Performance** runs the media, reads the numbers and decides what to scale next.

expandable.label: How the teams hand off
expandable.body: A brief starts in Strategy, moves to Creative for production, and lands in Performance for launch. Every Monday the three leads review one shared dashboard. Nobody owns a metric alone, which is why the handoff notes matter more than the org chart.

stat.label: median ROAS across retained accounts last quarter

cards.body: That figure is why clients stay. It is also why we treat every euro of ad spend as if it were our own.

cards.title: Mara Lindqvist, co-founder
cards.body: A good campaign is not the one with the prettiest ad. It is the one where we can explain, in one sentence, why the number moved.

cards.title: Every claim has a metric
cards.body:
When you say a campaign is *working*, you say which number says so and over what period.

If you can't name the metric, the claim is a feeling. Feelings are welcome in retros, not in client reports.

check.question: A teammate says the new video ads "feel strong". What's the right follow-up?

options.text: Ask which metric moved and over what period
Add the ads to the client report as a win
Scale the budget while the momentum lasts

check.explanation: At Brightline Media a claim without a metric is just an impression. Ask for the number first, then decide.

cards.title: What happens next
cards.body:
Tomorrow you'll shadow a Monday dashboard review with your team lead.

Before then, run through the **Metric deck** flashcards and the **Metric myths** quiz. Both take under ten minutes.

expandable.label: Your first-week checklist
expandable.body:
Day 1: accounts and tools access.

Day 2: shadow the Monday dashboard review.

Day 3: pair with Performance on one live account.

Day 5: present one observation from the account to your lead. One sentence, one metric.

feedback.complete: That's the lay of the land. Welcome aboard.

modules.title: The four departments
modules.instructions: Flip each card. Mark it **Got it** when you could explain it to a client.

cards.back: Turns the client's business goal into a measurable plan: audience, channels, budget split and KPIs.
Builds and runs the campaigns in the ad platforms. Owns bids, targeting, pacing and day-to-day optimisation.
Owns tracking, dashboards and reporting. If a number is on a slide, Analytics can tell you where it came from.
The client's single point of contact. Runs briefs, approvals, expectations and the weekly status call.
Designs ads and landing pages. Works with Strategy on messaging and with Media Buying on formats.
cards.hint: Not one of the four core departments, but you will work with them every week.

cards.back: Monday 10:00 all-hands: every account gives a 60-second update. Red / amber / green only — details go in the channel.

modules.title: How a campaign moves through the agency
modules.instructions: Select each stage to see who owns it, how long it takes and what has to be true before it starts.

stages.title: Client brief
stages.summary: Goals, audience, budget and timing are agreed.
stages.details:
The account manager runs a 45-minute briefing call and turns it into a one-page brief. A brief is only *done* when the client has signed off on the objective, the primary KPI and the budget.

Ambiguous briefs are the number one cause of rework later, so push back on vague goals like “more awareness” until they become measurable.
checklist: One measurable objective and primary KPI
Brief signed off by the client

stages.title: Strategy
stages.summary: Channels, messaging angles and a media split are proposed.
stages.details:
Strategy translates the brief into a plan: which channels, what the core message is, how the budget splits across them and what results are realistic.

The output is a short deck plus a media plan spreadsheet with projected reach, clicks and cost per result for each channel.

stages.title: Creative production
stages.summary: Copy, visuals and video are produced in every required format.
stages.details:
Designers and copywriters produce the assets listed in the media plan: static images, short video cuts and ad copy variants. Every asset is reviewed against the brand guide before it goes to the client.

Aim for at least **three** distinct concepts per audience so optimisation has something to choose between.
checklist: Assets exported in every placement size

stages.title: Tracking setup
stages.summary: Pixels, conversions and UTM naming are verified before spend starts.
stages.details:
Nothing launches without working measurement. Analytics installs or verifies pixels, defines conversion events and applies the agency UTM convention to every link.

A test conversion is recorded in each platform and in the client's analytics before the launch checklist is signed.
checklist: Pixels firing on all key pages
UTM parameters follow the naming convention

stages.title: Launch
stages.summary: Campaigns go live after a four-eyes check.
stages.details:
The media buyer builds the campaigns, a second person reviews targeting, budgets and links, and the campaigns go live. The first 24 hours are watched closely for delivery issues and disapproved ads.

The client gets a short launch confirmation with screenshots of the live ads.
checklist: Daily budgets match the media plan
Launch confirmation sent to the client

stages.title: Optimisation
stages.summary: Budgets and creative are adjusted weekly against the KPI.
stages.details: Each week the media buyer reviews performance against the plan, shifts budget towards what works and pauses what does not. Creative fatigue usually shows after two to three weeks: when frequency climbs and click-through drops, the team requests a creative refresh.
checklist: Creative refresh requested when fatigue appears

stages.title: Reporting
stages.summary: Results, learnings and next steps are shared with the client.
stages.details:
At the end of the flight the account team compiles a report: results against the KPI, what was learned about audiences and creative, and a recommendation for the next campaign.

The best reports lead with **three insights**, not thirty charts.
checklist: Report presented live to the client

modules.title: Where would you look?
modules.instructions: Three situations from your first week. Pick the best first move.

questions.prompt: A client asks for last month's ROAS on their search campaign. Where do you look first?

options.text: The Pulse Analytics dashboard for the account
options.explanation: Dashboards are the source of truth for performance numbers.

options.text: Ask the media buyer on Slack
options.explanation: Fine as a follow-up, but the number should already be in the dashboard.
The brief holds targets, not results.

questions.explanation: Numbers live in dashboards. Briefs hold goals. People explain context.

questions.prompt: You are not sure which naming convention to use for a new campaign.

options.explanation: Every convention is written down in the Playbook.

options.text: Invent a sensible name and fix it later
Copy whatever the last campaign used
options.explanation: The last campaign might be the exception, not the rule.

questions.hint: We write things down so nobody has to guess.

questions.prompt: Select everything that belongs in the client's shared channel.

options.text: Internal debates about the client's decisions

questions.explanation: If the client would be surprised to read it, it does not belong in a shared channel.
